Neonatal body mass in Mehely’s horseshoe bat Rhinolophus mehelyi has been measured at 3.4 grams [Wwb = 3.4 grams] for female pups, a value that is modest even among congeners of similar adult size. This low birth weight is consistent with an altricial developmental strategy in which newborns are highly dependent on maternal care during the early post-natal period. At the opposite end of the growth trajectory, adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of 12.6 grams [Wwi = 12.6 grams], a body mass that reflects the energetic demands of a temperate-zone insectivore that must balance thermoregulation with foraging activity. Field studies conducted in Mediterranean cave roosts indicate that this species exhibits a relatively slow life-history pace, with females producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and giving birth to only one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year]. This low reproductive output is characteristic of many rhinolophid bats and is thought to be linked to the constraints imposed by prolonged gestation and the extended period of lactation that follows parturition.

During the active period of the annual cycle, when body temperatures are maintained at approximately 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the gestation time for Rhinolophus mehelyi has been recorded at 90 days [tg = 90 days]. This interval, which is relatively prolonged for a bat of its body size, encompasses the full duration of embryogenesis and foetal development within the uterus. The extended gestational period likely reflects the need for sufficient foetal maturation given the constraints of a single-offspring reproductive strategy. Following delivery, the newborn pup enters a period of intense dependency during which it relies entirely on its mother’s milk for nourishment. The transition to nutritional independence occurs when the juvenile is weaned at 35 days after birth [tx = 35 days after birth], a timing that allows the female to begin replenishing her own energy reserves before the onset of the autumn mating season at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. These life-history timings have been confirmed through captive observations and field mark-recapture programs.

The time from birth to first reproduction is notably protracted in this species, reflecting a delayed onset of reproductive activity that is typical of long-lived, slow-breeding mammals. Under the same thermal regime of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] that characterizes the active metabolic period, female Rhinolophus mehelyi produce their first litter at 730 days after birth [tp = 730 days after birth]. This two-year delay before first parturition is thought to be linked to the time required for complete skeletal maturation and the development of proficient foraging skills necessary to support the energetic costs of pregnancy and lactation. The postponement of breeding until the third year of life means that a female must survive multiple winters before making her first reproductive contribution to the population. Such a strategy amplifies the importance of adult survival and highlights the vulnerability of this species to any factor that reduces longevity, such as habitat disturbance or climate-induced shifts in prey availability.

Maximum recorded longevity in Rhinolophus mehelyi, documented from long-term banding studies in southern European populations, reaches approximately 33 years [am = approximately 33 years] when individuals are experiencing the typical body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] during their active periods. This extreme lifespan places Mehely’s horseshoe bat among the most long-lived bat species relative to body size, a pattern that is believed to be underpinned by exceptionally low extrinsic mortality rates in cave-dwelling populations and the evolution of robust cellular maintenance mechanisms. The contrast between this long lifespan and the very low annual reproductive output of one pup per year underscores the bet-hedging life-history strategy that characterizes the species. Survival into advanced age allows a female to accumulate multiple reproductive events over a lifetime, mitigating the consequences of occasional breeding failures. Consequently, even small reductions in adult survival probability can have disproportionately large negative effects on population growth rates, a consideration critical for conservation planning.

Echolocation call structure and foraging ecology further distinguish Rhinolophus mehelyi from its more common congeners. This species employs a high-duty-cycle approach, emitting long, constant-frequency calls that are ideally suited for detecting fluttering prey in cluttered environments such as forest understories and cave entrances. The maintenance of such energetically costly echolocation behavior requires a high baseline metabolic rate, which is supported by the elevated body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] during periods of activity. Comparative studies have shown that the wing morphology of Mehely’s horseshoe bat, characterized by relatively broad wings and a low aspect ratio, confers maneuverability at the expense of speed, allowing it to glean insects from foliage as well as capture airborne prey. These morphological and physiological specializations, combined with the life-history constraints described above, make Rhinolophus mehelyi particularly sensitive to habitat fragmentation and prey depletion, factors that are increasingly relevant in the context of ongoing environmental change across its Mediterranean range.
